In 1539 the Italian abbot Afranio folded the long body back on itself and added three keys, and the first rough version appeared. In the early 17th century She'ertecai removed the metal funnel around the reed and created the dulcian, the soft-voiced bassoon. In 1624 the German composer Schütz gave it an independent part in No. 24 of his sacred songs. Works by Vivaldi, Mozart and Weber widened its use in solo and concerto writing. In 1843 Almenräder and Heckel made an 18-key bassoon, in 1847 Buffet and others made a 22-key one, in 1851 Sax took out a patent on a metal 24-key instrument, and in 1855 Triebert and Marzoli applied the Boehm system to make a 30-key bassoon.

The bassoon is a double-reed woodwind instrument of the Europe/France culture area, with a range that covers the tenor and bass registers. The instrument is usually made of wood and comes apart into six pieces: the reed, the bocal, the wing joint, the boot, the long joint and the bell. The body folds back on itself in a U shape, with a total sounding length of about 2.54 m and a standing height of about 1.34 m. The player wraps both lips over the reed and blows directly, setting the reed vibrating; there are two modern fingering systems, French and German. Its music is mostly written at sounding pitch, usually in the bass and tenor clefs. A player is called a bassoonist, and the instrument appears in orchestras, wind bands and chamber music, and occasionally in pop, rock and jazz.
低音管音色深沉而富有表現力，具有獨特的溫暖質感。其低音域結實有力、渾厚飽滿，中高: The bassoon's timbre is deep and expressive, with a warmth of its own. Its low register is firm and strong, full and resonant; the middle and upper registers carry a soft resonance like a baritone voice, and the instrument is at once dramatic and lyrical. Because the double reed vibrates, the bassoon gives out a warm low-frequency resonance: the sound is neither too bright nor too dark, but has a mellow, deep grain. Next to the cello the bassoon's timbre is more penetrating and more of an individual; next to the horn it is steadier and more reserved. These traits let it both underpin the bass part and, in solo passages, show fine musical expression; it is an indispensable colour in the orchestra.

To make a sound, both lips roll over the reed and direct air pressure sets the reed vibrating. Beginners mostly use reeds made by a professional or a teacher; advanced players adjust them to their own style, or make their own. Playing needs a good grasp of the complicated keywork, and attention to how the length of the bocal and the state of the reed affect intonation and timbre.

Metal instruments were made in the past as well. The vibrating reed is made of cane, and plastic reeds also exist. The bocal is a metal tube with cork wrapped round its end, and the Heckel system offers German soft silver, soft-tone alloy, German hard silver, brass, high-purity jewellery silver and gold. Other parts include the metal connector where the boot folds back, cotton or linen thread for binding the reed, and nitrocellulose glue, beeswax, clear nail polish, hot-melt glue, epoxy or heat-shrink tubing for sealing it.
